planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; give full sun for the deepest winter bronze-red color.

directions: Compacta is an older, upright nandina selection valued for its dense, finely textured foliage and taller narrow habit compared to the wild species, making it a workhorse for privacy screening and background hedging. New growth emerges with a soft pink-bronze tinge, matures to medium green through summer, and shifts to bronzy-red in cool fall and winter weather. Clusters of small white flowers appear in late spring, followed by heavy sets of bright red berries that persist into winter and are an important food source for birds; however, the berries and foliage contain cyanogenic compounds and are toxic if ingested by pets, livestock, or grazing wildlife, so avoid planting where animals browse. It tolerates a wide range of soils provided they drain well and needs little supplemental water once established. Some regions consider Nandina domestica potentially invasive due to bird-dispersed seed, so check local guidance before planting near natural areas.

common_name: Umpqua Princess Nandina (Fine-Textured Tall Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in sun to shade; provide regular water the first season to establish the sturdy cane structure.

directions: Part of the sturdy-stemmed Umpqua series bred for strong upright canes, Umpqua Princess is a tall selection with larger leaves and narrower leaflets than its sibling Umpqua Chief, giving it a finer, lusher texture. Foliage is bright green through the warm months and takes on red and orange tones in winter, while summer brings clusters of small white flowers. Like other nandinas, its berries and foliage contain cyanogenic glycosides that are toxic to cats, dogs, and grazing animals, so site it away from areas where pets browse or livestock graze. It performs in exposures from full sun to fairly deep shade and adapts to average garden soil as long as drainage is adequate. Because Nandina domestica can naturalize from bird-spread seed in mild climates, gardeners in regions where it is flagged as invasive should check local extension guidance before planting.

common_name: Moyer's Red Nandina (Cold-Hardy Fall-Color Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; summer irrigation intensifies the fall and winter foliage color.

directions: Moyer's Red is an upright, fine-textured nandina prized for exceptionally reliable and long-lasting fall color, with foliage turning a rich reddish-purple that holds from early autumn well into spring in cooler climates. Cream and pink summer flowers give way to orange-red berries that attract birds; however, both berries and foliage contain cyanogenic compounds and should be kept away from pets and grazing animals due to toxicity risk. This cultivar tolerates occasional drought once established but colors up best with regular moisture and rich, well-drained soil, and it is noted for handling urban pollution and confined planting sites better than many shrubs. Because nandina seed is bird-dispersed and the species is regulated or discouraged as invasive in some regions, confirm local status before planting near wildlands.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; hot summers produce the heaviest, longest-lasting berry set.

directions: Richmond is a self-fertile, semi-evergreen nandina grown chiefly for its abundant, showy clusters of bright red berries that persist through autumn and winter, following cone-shaped panicles of small white summer flowers. Small lance-shaped leaflets color to burgundy-red in cold weather, adding to the winter display alongside the fruit. All parts, especially the berries, contain cyanogenic compounds that are toxic to cats, dogs, and grazing livestock, so avoid siting this cultivar where pets or animals have access to fallen fruit. It performs reliably in average, well-drained garden soil with low supplemental water once established and tolerates a range of light from full sun to part shade. Because its heavy berry production can be spread by birds, Richmond should be planted with awareness of regional invasiveness guidance for Nandina domestica.
